content: Acute bacterial meningitis is a condition associated with high rates of mortality and long-term complications. However, timely and appropriate antimicrobial and supportive treatments have significantly improved survival rates, particularly in infants and children. One critical aspect of supportive care is the careful management of fluid and electrolyte balance. Both excessive hydration and insufficient hydration can lead to poor outcomes. This review aimed to assess the impact of different volumes of fluid administration during the initial 72 hours of treatment for acute bacterial meningitis on mortality and neurological outcomes. The review represents the latest update of a study originally published in 2005, with subsequent updates in 2008 and 2014. For the 2016 update, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Acute Respiratory Infections Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Global Health, and Web of Science, up to March 2016. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different fluid volumes in the initial management of bacterial meningitis. The review included three trials involving a total of 420 children. No studies involving adult populations were identified. The largest trial was conducted in high-mortality settings and was deemed to have a low risk of bias in most domains, except for performance bias, which was rated as high risk. The other two trials were smaller and of lower quality. The meta-analysis revealed no significant difference between the maintenance-fluid group and the restricted-fluid group in terms of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.53 to 1.27; 407 participants; low-quality evidence) or acute severe neurological complications (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.08; 407 participants; low-quality evidence). However, when specific neurological outcomes were analyzed, the maintenance-fluid group showed statistically significant benefits. These included reduced rates of spasticity (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.93; 357 participants) and fewer seizures at 72 hours (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.83; 357 participants) and at 14 days (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.88; 357 participants). For chronic severe neurological sequelae at three months, there was very low-quality evidence suggesting a benefit of maintenance fluids over restricted fluids (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.89; 351 participants). The authors concluded that the overall quality of evidence regarding fluid therapy in children with acute bacterial meningitis is low to very low. There is insufficient evidence to definitively recommend maintenance fluids over restricted fluids in clinical practice. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to provide clearer guidance on this issue.
